initial_prompt: Write a short noir-style monologue about a lost sock.

messages.content: Write a short noir-style monologue about a lost sock.

They say it’s the heat that makes you crazy, but in this racket, it’s the spin. 

One minute we were swimming in suds, a perfect pair of argyles tangled in a wet embrace. Then came the darkness. The tumbler. A hot, screaming vortex of cotton and synthetic blends. I held on as long as I could, fighting the static, fighting the pull of a heavy denim jean that didn't care who it crushed.

When the buzzer sounded, the silence hit harder than the fall. I tumbled out into the plastic basket, breathless, searching through the heap of towels and undershirts. Nothing. Just a cloud of gray lint and a lonely dryer sheet.

I checked the trap. I checked the gap behind the machine—the graveyard of good intentions. He was gone. Maybe he made a break for it, hitched a ride inside a pant leg, or maybe the machine just swallowed him whole. Now I’m sitting here in the top drawer, surrounded by singletons and rejects, waiting for a foot that’ll never come. In this town, you’re either a pair, or you’re a dust rag. And my elastic is starting to give.

It was raining. Or maybe the washer was just leaking again. Who knows in this damp, mildew-scented town.

She was a high-class dame. Seventy percent Merino wool, reinforced heel, breathable mesh. A real catch. We were sole-mates. We walked the same streets, smelled the same feet. We were a pair. Until the Agitation Cycle.

I told her to stay close to the towels. "Towels are safe," I said. "They don't have zippers. Zippers are bad news, doll. They got teeth." But she wouldn't listen. She had eyes for a red hoodie who looked like he was gonna bleed on everyone.

Then came the dryer. That hot, tumbling hellscape. I blacked out somewhere between 'Damp Dry' and 'Permanent Press.' When I woke up, I was static-clinging to a pair of tighty-whities three sizes too big for me. I felt cheap.

I searched the lint trap. Nothing but gray fuzz and a button that knew too much. I asked the dryer sheet, but he was washed up, devoid of scent, completely drained.

So here I am. Solo. A bachelor in a drawer full of widows. Waiting for the day the Big Guy decides I’m no longer useful as footwear and turns me into a hand puppet for the kid. God, I hope they don’t draw eyes on me with a Sharpie. I don’t think I could look myself in the mirror.
